title: The poisoned arrow
hookLine: the Buddha: a wounded man won't wait to learn who shot him before the arrow comes out (Majjhima Nikaya 63)

cards: Something goes wrong. The deal falls through, the diagnosis comes back, the text you didn't want arrives. And right away the questions come.
Why did this happen? Whose fault is it? What does it mean about my life?
Was it always going to go this way? Some of them matter. But while they're spinning, the actual hurt is still sitting there, untouched.
The Buddha had a picture for this.

teach.b: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, the Majjhima Nikaya, number sixty-three. A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, stewing. There are big questions the Buddha has never answered.
Is the universe eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or not? Is the soul the same as the body?
What happens to an awakened one after death? So he gives the Buddha an ultimatum: answer these, or I'm leaving. The Buddha starts with a question of his own: did I ever promise you I'd answer them?

teach.h: A MAN SHOT WITH A POISONED ARROW.
teach.b: A man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: no one pulls this arrow out until I know who shot me.
Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What was his name, his family? Tall or short, dark or fair?
What village? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow?
What was the string made of, and what feathers were on the arrow? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he learned any of it.

teach.h: FIRST THE WOUND, THEN THE QUESTIONS.
teach.b: He doesn't call the questions foolish. He says the holy life isn't built on answering them: they don't lead to calm, or to awakening.

What he teaches instead is suffering, where it comes from, its ending, and the path to that ending: the wound, and how to heal it. Buddhist teachers read his silence on those questions in more than one way.
But the order in the story is clear.
First, the arrow comes out. The questions can come after, if they still seem urgent.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set aside certain metaphysical questions and focused on suffering and its ending.

o: the poison smeared on the arrow's tip
the surgeon who comes to treat the wound
the arrow in the Buddha's wounded-man story

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: answer my questions, or I leave
won't let the arrow out yet

s: the Buddha calls Malunkyaputta's questions foolish
he says they don't lead to peace, and teaches the wound and its healing instead.
the wounded man wants to know what feathers were on the arrow
and the bow, the string, the shooter's name, height and village.
the Buddha had promised Malunkyaputta answers to these questions
he asks: did I ever say, come, and I will answer them? he never had.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a monk says: answer whether the universe is eternal, or I'm leaving. what do you do?
o: ask if you ever promised to answer, and tell of an arrow
let him go without a word
games.why: he asks whether he ever promised to answer those questions, then tells of a man shot with a poisoned arrow who dies waiting to learn who shot him.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that's hurting a little today, not the biggest, and notice the why questions that come with it: whose fault, what it means, how it happened. Set them to one side; they'll keep.
Then ask a smaller question, what would help this hurt right now, a glass of water, an apology, a walk, a phone call, a rest, and picture doing it.

wordCard.voice: Salla. The Pali word for the arrow in the Buddha's picture of a wounded man who wants every answer before he'll let the surgeon help.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: salla, an arrow or dart, the word for the barb in the Buddha's picture.

carryVoice: Your line: pull the arrow. The why can wait until the wound is tended. That's day seventy-six.
